title: Lambda Calculus
body:
Alonzo Church's model of computation, from 1936, the same year as the
[[Turing Machine]] and developed independently. It has no states, no tape, and no memory: just
functions, and the rule for applying them. It computes exactly what a Turing machine computes,
which is the main piece of evidence for the Church-Turing thesis.

## The whole syntax

Three forms, and that is genuinely all of it:

| Form | Written | Means |
|---|---|---|
| variable | $x$ | a name |
| abstraction | $\lambda x. M$ | the function taking $x$ to $M$ |
| application | $M\ N$ | apply $M$ to $N$ |

$\lambda x. x$ is the identity function. $\lambda x. \lambda y. x$ takes two arguments and
returns the first. Functions take one argument; multiple arguments are done by returning
another function, which is **currying**.

## Beta reduction

Computation is one rule: substitute the argument for the parameter.

$$(\lambda x. M)\ N \to M[x := N]$$

```
(λx. x x) (λy. y)
=> (λy. y) (λy. y)
=> (λy. y)
```

Reduce until nothing can be reduced, and that **normal form** is the answer. Some terms have
none: $(\lambda x. x x)(\lambda x. x x)$ reduces to itself forever, which is this system's
version of an infinite loop, and it is not a coincidence that the halting problem shows up
here too. See [[Undecidability]]; whether two lambda terms are equivalent is undecidable, and
that was Church's original result.

Alpha conversion (renaming bound variables) exists so that substitution does not accidentally
capture a name, and eta conversion says $\lambda x. f x$ is the same function as $f$.

## Encoding everything out of nothing

The system has no numbers, no booleans, and no data structures. You build them from functions,
which is the part worth understanding:

```
Church numerals: n is "apply f n times"
  0 = λf. λx. x
  1 = λf. λx. f x
  2 = λf. λx. f (f x)

Booleans: pick one of two arguments
  true  = λx. λy. x
  false = λx. λy. y
  if    = λb. λt. λe. b t e
```

`if` needs no special form: `true` already *is* the choosing behaviour. [[Recursion]] comes
from the Y combinator, a term that hands a function itself, so even recursion is not primitive.

## Why the course cares

Turing machines and lambda calculus were built by different people, in different formalisms,
in the same year, to answer the same question, and they turned out to define exactly the same
class of computable functions. That convergence is why the Church-Turing thesis is believed.
General recursive functions, register machines, and [[Cellular Automata]] all land in the same
place. A system that can simulate one of them is **Turing complete**.

Note it is not just an equivalent model, it is the more *usable* one. Reasoning about a
program's meaning by tracing tape cells is unpleasant; substitution is the ordinary way we
already think about functions.

## Where it went

Lambda calculus is the theory functional programming is a dialect of, so this note points
forward at [[PROGRAMMING PARADIGMS]]. Lisp (1958) was the first language built on it, and the
inheritance is direct and visible:

- anonymous functions, still called lambdas in Python, Java, C#, and JavaScript
- first-class and higher-order functions, `map` and `filter`
- closures
- currying and partial application, the default in Haskell and ML
- Hindley-Milner type inference, which is typed lambda calculus applied

## Core Facts to Know

- Three constructs: variable, abstraction $\lambda x. M$, application $M\ N$.
- Beta reduction $(\lambda x. M) N \to M[x := N]$ is the only computation rule.
- Functions take exactly one argument; more is done by currying.
- Alpha conversion renames bound variables to avoid capture; eta says $\lambda x. f x = f$.
- A term in **normal form** cannot be reduced further; some terms never reach one.
- Numbers, booleans, and recursion are all *encoded*, not built in.
- Church numerals encode $n$ as "apply $f$ $n$ times".
- The Y combinator provides recursion.
- Lambda calculus is exactly as powerful as a [[Turing Machine]]: this is the Church-Turing thesis's main evidence.
- Church published in 1936, the same year as Turing, independently.
- Lambda-term equivalence is undecidable.
- Functional programming languages are direct descendants.
